reason: Five words of narrative connective, and the resemblance is closer than it deserves to be: Mark 16:3's women say among themselves, as they go, 'Who shall roll us away the stone?' and Helaman 9:1's five men say among themselves, as they go, that they will know of a surety whether Nephi is a prophet. Both parties are walking toward a body they have not yet seen. But the shared words are all frame and no content, the KJV uses 'said among themselves' of half a dozen crowds, and nothing else in Helaman 9 touches the resurrection narrative. Recorded because the situational parallel is the kind a careful reader would stop over.

A genuine temptation, considered and declined. 'Know of a surety' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 15:13 and Acts 12:11, and Acts 12:11 is attractive because Peter says it having just been brought out of prison by an angel, which is where the five men of Helaman 9 are about to end up. The contact is four words of idiom with no other element in common: Helaman's speakers use it of a test they are about to run, Peter of a deliverance already accomplished, and there is no angel, no chains and no gate in the Book of Mormon chapter. The chapter's prison borrowings are at 9:9, from Acts 16:23 and Matthew 14:3, and they are verbally much stronger.

Four words of which three are auxiliaries and a pronoun. Hebrews 11:6's 'he that cometh to God must believe that he is' concerns believing that God exists; Helaman 9:2's 'we do not believe that he is a prophet' concerns an office. The window closes one word early in the way ADJUDICATING §4 describes — Hebrews' next word is 'and', Helaman's is 'a'.

Six words of subordinating tissue joining a verb to its result clause. 2 Samuel 22:39 is David consuming his enemies so that they could not arise; Helaman 9:8 is the crowd supposing God smote the five so that they could not flee. Recorded rather than passed over because the run is long and because a reader might hear a divine-smiting parallel in it; there is none, and the Book of Mormon clause is the crowd's mistaken inference, which the chapter then refutes.

sharedText: it came to pass that on the morrow
reason: A nine-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is worth nothing. 'And it came to pass that on the morrow' is the Book of Mormon's standard temporal transition and the KJV's; Numbers 17:8 is Aaron's rod budding in the tabernacle. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names first — a long run means nothing on its own — and it is the clearest instance of it in Helaman 7-9. Malachi 4:5's 'of the great and' and 1 Kings 13:29's 'to mourn and to' are ranked at the same verse and excluded on the same evidence; neither is given a separate entry.

Five words of reported-speech frame. Luke 9:10 is the apostles returning and telling Jesus all that they had done; Helaman 9:13 is five prisoners telling the judges all that they had done. The construction is the KJV's ordinary way of summarizing a report and carries no signal. The chapter's real Gospel borrowing at this point in the trial is at 9:19.

sharedText: the man that hath done this
reason: A five-word run and a real temptation, because 2 Samuel 12:5 is David's furious verdict on the rich man of Nathan's parable — 'the man that hath done this thing shall surely die' — and it is famously a verdict the speaker has unwittingly passed on himself. Helaman 9:20's judges ask Nephi 'who is this man that hath done this murder?', and 9:27-38 will reveal that the murderer is one of their own band. The parallel is real and the wording is not: Helaman's clause is an interrogative asking for a name, 2 Samuel's a demonstrative pronouncing a sentence, and the Book of Mormon has no parable, no Nathan, and no self-conviction. Filed as wrong-sense with the note that a reader who wants the Nathan resonance should have it as resonance, not as a source.

Five words of pure direction-giving. Ecclesiastes 7:2's 'It is better to go to the house of mourning' is an aphorism about mortality; Helaman 9:26 sends men to a named man's house to ask him a question. Nothing else shared.

One of the KJV's commonest theological phrases and one of the Book of Mormon's. Ephesians 3:7's 'given unto me by the effectual working of his power' and John 6:65's 'except it were given unto him of my Father' were ranked alongside it and are excluded on the same evidence; none is given a separate entry. The verse's interesting relation is not to any of them but to Acts 8:10's 'the great power of God', which the Samaritans say of Simon Magus and which Nephi here refuses to let stand of himself — that is argued on the link at 9:16.

Four words, of which the content is a passive verb every prophet in both testaments uses of himself. John 3:28 is the Baptist disclaiming the Christ and saying he is sent before him; Helaman 9:36 is Nephi claiming honesty and divine commission. The disclaimer structure is superficially similar and the vocabulary is not distinctive enough to adjudicate.

sharedText: the words which he had said unto them
reason: Seven words of reported-speech frame, ranked highest at the verse. Genesis 45:27 is the brothers telling Jacob all Joseph's words; the run is the frame and the content is elsewhere in both verses. 1 Kings 13:11, Judges 20:40 and 2 Peter 3:15 are ranked at the same verse on runs of the same kind and are excluded on the same evidence; none is given a separate entry.

'Set at liberty' occurs in four KJV verses — Jeremiah 34:16, Luke 4:18, Acts 26:32 and Hebrews 13:23 — and Luke 4:18's 'to set at liberty them that are bruised' is the memorable one. It is declined as a source because Luke's phrase renders a programmatic quotation of Isaiah 61 and Helaman's is a procedural note about five men leaving a cell; Acts 26:32's 'this man might have been set at liberty' is closer in setting and equally undecidable. Three words of legal idiom with four candidate verses and no way to choose. The release is recorded instead on the Acts 16:23 link at 9:9, where the whole prison sequence is argued.
